Kain on how an AI found a simpler way to move tokens to the DAO in about 7 seconds, one his team had never thought of

"Whenever we considered something like this, it was like we would have to change the token state. But no, actually, this is a much more elegant solution that the clanker found in, like, seven seconds."

"You spent your whole life doing this, and then the clanker is just so much smarter than you. It was like, why don't you just use the token authority to create an approval to transfer the tokens?"

"And I was like, no. We can't do that. That wouldn't work. And one of the guys is like, Opus is pretty convinced that it would work."

"Create a new approval, and then transfer the tokens to the DAO. It was so simple, and it just never had occurred to us."

LlamaRisk's Adam Sadowski on why Aave froze markets after the Binance hack, even though nothing was stolen from it

"There's nuance to the situation that I think a lot of people are missing. They hear Aave is associated in some way. Does this mean Aave had funds stolen from it? And the answer is a resounding no."

"There was nothing that was stolen from Aave. The protocol itself worked as it was intended, which is that users can supply collateral and create an over-collateralized loan, maintaining the solvency of the protocol, so suppliers to the lending market can always withdraw their money."

"What we're concerned about is that Aave doesn't wanna have stolen funds on its books, although it's not actually interfering with the protocol operation in any way. So that's why we needed to take action."

Martin Casado:

"I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that, because it was always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. 

The biggest shift with AI is I can take 20 people, give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Do they make 500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new.

We've turned this into a capital resourcing problem, and we're capital allocators. We're in this very strategic position to help drive the future in a much more direct way than we ever have been before.

If you look at Anthropic and OpenAI, they've probably raised more money in aggregate than the entire downstream ecosystem combined. 

They are these mechanisms of turning money into growth."

a16z's Martin Casado on the four mindsets people bring to investing, and why knowing yours stops you from justifying your own bias:

1. Financial

"The correct proxy for the health of a business is the market it's going into and its finances. That's what it is. What are the SaaS metrics? What is the size of the market? That is a proxy for the entire business."

2. Productive

"You believe you're investing in a productive asset, and the productive asset is what's creating value. If you believe in that, as it creates value, it will create market... The type of diligence you do if you're a productive investor is more like, what is the technical approach? What are the adjacent markets?"

3. Frontier

"I think this is the romantic, idealized version of VC from the 60s and 70s, which is kind of YOLO. It's like, founders know better than VCs, and they've seen something that I don't see, and they're gonna go out there and do it. And, like, who am I to second guess them?"

4. Speculative

"It is always so surprising how prevalent it is... They don't even care about the asset. They just want to time a market, right?... They're like, 'Well, this looks cheap. It's clearly gonna go up in value' or, 'This is the top of the market, like, I'm gonna get out.'"

"...You can justify any deal or not justify any deal. So if you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always basically just kind of justify whatever personal bias you have."

@martin_casado w/ @patrick_oshag on @InvestLikeBest

a16z's Anish Acharya and David Pawlan, creator of Assistant Benchmark, on the gap between people's stated and revealed preferences on privacy, and what that means for AI agent adoption:

"I think in revealed preferences, consumers will share any amount of data for even the most trivial amount of upside."

"People have been connecting their cards, their credit cards, and their bank accounts via Plaid since the Venmo era. But when you ask them, they're like, 'Oh, yes, I'm very concerned about trust and safety.'"

"I think an example though of where consumers are very concerned about sort of trust and assumptions is around being embarrassed and social signaling... The social mechanics actually feel so much higher stakes than the actual, like, real-world implications."

"[One company] offered a million dollars worth of pizza to anyone that wanted to use their product... In order to get that $30 of pizza, you were granting access to your entire Google Workspace, all of your emails, all of your data for 30 bucks."

"It just proves it right there, that people are willing to just give up all that data for some free pizza."

@illscience @DavidPawlan

The era of massive Big Tech stock buybacks is over.

Combined buybacks by Alphabet, $GOOGL, Amazon, $AMZN, Microsoft, $MSFT, Meta, $META, and Oracle, $ORCL, fell to $4.4 billion in Q3 2026, the lowest since Q3 2017.

This comes as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle have not purchased their own stock in 2026.

By comparison, combined buybacks by these Big Tech companies stood at +$33.0 billion in Q1 2026.

AI spending is coming at the expense of Big Tech buybacks.

Top-quartile venture beat top-quartile buyout through the internet buildout and again through mobile and cloud, and a16z's Jen Kha argues we're at the start of the next wave.

Tech buyouts have long been the "safe" bet in private markets. Now the stress is showing:

- In the first half of 2026, venture funds marked their tech holdings up 16%, while buyout funds marked theirs down 4%

- 70% of the debt foreclosed in 2025 and 2026 came from deals done in 2021 or 2022

- A typical buyout now needs 10 to 12% EBITDA growth a year to make 2.5x in five years, up from about 5% in 2015

- Top 5% venture funds from 2007-16 returned 5.3x their capital in cash, versus 3.5x for top 5% buyout funds

"Tech buyout is a late-cycle asset class. It's most effective once a technology wave has settled and when business models are predictable enough to borrow against. When a new technology wave drops, all bets are off. By contrast, that's when venture shines."

Full piece from a16z's Jen Kha: https://t.co/FQ7O8OwBe3

Cyberoffense/defense is probably going to eat up a TON of compute and end up a continuous compute-intensive arms race. 

Even $AMZN CEO thinks cybersecurity would take up 20% of tokens consumed for the next year. 

It's literally a problem of how much you throw at compute for vulnerability discovery + model capability, from of my chats w/ Horizon3. 

And this is going to become a nation state issue, as seen with the implications already with PHP to vulnerabilities with banks/infrastructure from AI swarms. 

But people see this and throw money at $CRWD, $NET, and others, which I was saying was a bubble. 

If it's a compute issue, the economics go to the infra, from neoclouds to $NBIS to networking like $AAOI. 

We'll likely see swarms go wild from aggressor nation states in the next few years. 

And any country, whether that's Japan or EU that don't have their own capabilities might suffer severe damage. 

US spent $11T+ cumulatively (inflation adjusted) on Nuclear weapons and we're like ~$1.8T into the the "cyber-nuclear weapon" equivalent of that

And this is not even including the endless other economic implications from AI in other fields from advancing cancer discovery to workforce automation with physical AI. 

It's hard to measure AI sustainability if $50K in compute spend from a foreign actor can take down $10B of your own infrastructure. 

AI has become a bipartisan national security issue, and even Democrats would not want China overtake the US in this field.

tweets.text:
For companies like $SIVE / $AAOI, the demand imbalance for lasers are so severe

That even a 20-30% overall demand reduction from a hypothetical DC slowdown would likely not eliminate the shortage. 

We're seeing this before the next architectural shifts, where $NVDA Jensen Huang expects 15x optical volume for CPO scale-up. 

And as more hyperscalers commit to NPO as seen with $LITE new $5B UHP laser contracts. 

I'd argue this is more nuanced since I can't say the same for finished 800G/1.6T pluggables or lower end 70mW-100mW laser ranges that are currently bottlenecks. 

But this argument is more toward higher spec lasers. 

$AAOI is vertically integrated and has 300-400 mW capabilities, so they have the capability to shift attention to merchant lasers over supplying end-to-end optical transceivers. 

$SIVE is more pure play on this laser bottleneck, but they have the capabilities for 200mW + higher margin multiwavelength NPO/CPO lasers. 

I'd argue this is specifically the case for bottlenecks where demand imbalances are so deep (creating higher long term visibility, such as HBM). 

Whether it's large body substrates from $ATS that's bottlenecking Marvell + $AMD or lasers from $LITE that are sold out into 2029. 

or liquid transformers that have 4-5 year lead times. 

They they would still sell out of capacity even if overall demand decreased. 

If markets de-risked, it would make sense to hit optical module manufacturing players, maybe server rack assembly, to companies that still require heavy financing like Neoclouds.

And obviously haircut growth valuations (but not to the point where demand collapses to 0).

Yet we're seeing everything in AI trade is getting lumped up together as something that requires heavy financing + not profitable.

That even a 20-30% overall demand reduction from a hypothetical DC slowdown would likely not eliminate the shortage. 

We're seeing this before the next architectural shifts, where $NVDA Jensen Huang expects 15x optical volume for CPO scale-up. 

And as more hyperscalers commit to NPO as seen with $LITE new $5B UHP laser contracts. 

I'd argue this is more nuanced since I can't say the same for finished 800G/1.6T pluggables or lower end 70mW-100mW laser ranges that are currently bottlenecks. 

But this argument is more toward higher spec lasers. 

$AAOI is vertically integrated and has 300-400 mW capabilities, so they have the capability to shift attention to merchant lasers over supplying end-to-end optical transceivers. 

$SIVE is more pure play on this laser bottleneck, but they have the capabilities for 200mW + higher margin multiwavelength NPO/CPO lasers. 

I'd argue this is specifically the case for bottlenecks where demand imbalances are so deep (creating higher long term visibility, such as HBM). 

Whether it's large body substrates from $ATS that's bottlenecking Marvell + $AMD or lasers from $LITE that are sold out into 2029. 

or liquid transformers that have 4-5 year lead times. 

They they would still sell out of capacity even if overall demand decreased. 

If markets de-risked, it would make sense to hit optical module manufacturing players, maybe server rack assembly, to companies that still require heavy financing like Neoclouds.

And obviously haircut growth valuations (but not to the point where demand collapses to 0).

Yet we're seeing everything in AI trade is getting lumped up together as something that requires heavy financing + not profitable.

With $AXTI, even if demand was cut 50%, they'd still likely be sold out.

Since customers are asking for 3x+ their contracted volumes. I'd argue InP substrates are just as severe as lasers. 

In just 90 days, $AXTI literally went from:

Q2 backlog: $100m 
Q3 backlog: $500m+

With an extra $300-$400m+ from ordinary business, not multi-year agreements from $LITE / $COHR. 

I'm sure there's some double ordering but the materials are just so cheap relative to overall BOM, that it's spare change.

tweets.text:
Little rant, but to show you how rampant deleveraging has become:

- $CIFR is worth 44% LESS than when they announced their initial $GOOGL / $AMZN colo deals. 

- $AAOI is now ~ the same price BEFORE they secured major hyperscaler orders, raised $1.6B for capacity expansion and gave their suprising initial -> $378M+ projection ->  ~$471M revenue forecast.

- $ESMT ($2B MC) is the perfect example representing the memory sector.

B-BUT AI NAMES ARE NOT PROFITABLE??? Q3 Earnings: $526.2M gross profit, $330M net income.

To give you a comparison of what that looks like, the net income of $CRWD ($251B MC) was literally $5.3M. 

$NOW ($113B MC) was $277M.
$TSLA ($1.5T) was $787M.

Different industries/durability, but if we care about what's actually hitting the balance sheet: 

ESMT is sitting on ~$937M in net assets ($740M net cash, $278M inventory, etc), so EV goes down to $1.2B ish.

Annualized P/E: 1.6x...

People keep saying "Peak Earnings", "Cyclical", "no moat" but who in the world would want to build an old ass DDR2 line + fab and qualify it?

From ESMT commentary, we'll likely see ASP hikes Q4 to make up for potential consumer demand dropping. 

And further supply tightening with Samsung/Micron discontinuing DDR2/DDR3 lines.

Winbond was leaving DDR2 lines to pursue higher end memory. People keep saying China, but even Gigadevice was leaving DDR3 to pursue higher end memory. "DDR3's share of our DRAM revenue will continue to decline until we eventually stop selling DDR3 products."Nanya discontinued DDR2 lines few days ago. 

This is while majority of ESMT revenue comes from DDR2/DDR3. In ~3 quarters of constant earnings, ESMT would have more assets than their entire MC.

Who is going to stop buying $40 DLink cameras if their $3 memory cost goes to $3.5?

$MU / Samsung / $SKHY / $SNDK share similar parallels where durability is contractually enforced via take/pay LTAs with price floors.

But markets are pretending that it just won't happen, despite Samsung already being the most profitable company in the world. 

Markets should care about how much FCF is actually hitting the balance sheets, but are just indiscriminately selling off everything now.

But continue rotating capital into 47x P/E companies like Walmart or 180x forward P/E names like $CRWD.

thread_tweets.text:
If a company is valued at $2B, has ~$1B in cash/inventory... And makes $354M FCF a quarter. 

Then returns 30-50% of FCF for dividends next year. 

I'd argue it's more of a matter of time before shareholder returns/fundamentals, (especially memory) overpower forced selling. 

But stock prices can look really dislocated from actual performance for periods of time, like now. 

Same with photonics, but that's more of a 2027-2028 growth type story with CPO + more optical content/xpu.

Laser companies like $LITE, $AAOI, and potentially $SIVE depending on quals, would likely be printing few years after capacity expansion comes online.

And it's already been largely funded... Lumentum with $NVDA + hyperscalers, AOI with $1.6B+ in ATMs, Sivers with 700M SEK from institutions. 

Compared to other sectors that still require a lot of capital for their buildouts.

I'll summarize my views: 

- tariffs were dumb and a huge unforced error. even if economic impact was largely de minimis, they are still an easy target for the left

- Trump crypto ventures: obviously a huge problem and a foreseeable mistake. I personally objected to this loudly, even before he was elected (look up my name and WLF or the trump memecoin in google news). I was very critical on this point  

- immigration: I support the crackdown, think Trump could have done it more elegantly, but undeniably he delivered on what he said he would, no complaints. maybe was unpopular due to inherent demographics of this country, but not something I am complaining about. 

- Iran war: unforced error. Though I support what he is doing, I think he should have gone much harder much quicker, rather than leave us with this stalemate causing high gas prices. Optics disaster undeniably. 

- Affordability: his decisions didn't help at the margin, but in terms of economic growth (not solely within his control), he has been pretty good. The economy isn't as bad as people think it is. 

- AI: WH hasn't done much one way or the other. Dems have the benefit of being the AI skeptic and datacenter skeptic party. They are on the wrong side of that in my view, but it is politically popular for now.

That legal paralysis allowed De Jong to get away with one of the biggest bank heists in history. If regulators had left me in charge of my bank, no customer funds would have been lost. But because the Puerto Rican government took over, tens of millions of dollars in customer funds will be lost or stolen.

if you just barely care about the privacy sector, I highly recommend listening to this to understand how huge Arcium is and why.

the reason most companies still don't run AI on their real data is simple: they don't trust whoever is running the model.

hospitals won't put patient records into OpenAI. banks won't hand over their books. and obviously they're right not to.

Arcium just recently released Blackthorn which is solving exactly this. you can run inference on sensitive data, and the operator never sees it in plaintext. not the cloud, not the operator, not even Arcium itself.

as @yrschrade is also mentioning, that's the part every other "private AI" project is still faking and essentially just larping about. most of them rely on hardware enclaves that have already been exploited more than once. Blackthorn replaces that trust with actual cryptography via MPCs, running on standard NVIDIA GPUs.

people should have this way higher on their radar. it's what finally unlocks AI for healthcare, finance, law and government.

AI for enterprises, with trillions in data that has been sitting on the sidelines because there was never a safe way to use it.

only possible on @Arcium.

Key Takeaways:
>Bitcoin and gold are outperforming post-election while tech lags. The Bitcoin-NASDAQ correlation breaking down is affirming. 
>More spending and debt issuance under a divided government is likely to keep the lights and the debt ceiling raised. Rs no longer have the numbers for their austerity wing to achieve anything. That's a bullish backdrop for Bitcoin as a hard asset as a meaningful percentage of the electorate and our trading partners object not only to the magnitude of deficits but also the use of funds.
>Bitcoin’s regulatory picture is already clear. Nothing changes post-election. Custody and leverage are both regulated. Adoption continues to grow, with Bhutan becoming the third country to hold Bitcoin on its central bank balance sheet and Israel considering using BTC to circumvent some sanctions which are probably more likely given the elections' outcome.
>VanEck sees Bitcoin setting up for another major run. It      follows a predictable four-year cycle, and based on that pattern, the bottom came in October. Democrats don’t create regulatory uncertainty for Bitcoin. Debate around altcoins and stablecoins is a separate story.
>Bitcoin miners hit by Texas data center approvals may be a buying opportunity. Many stocks have round-tripped since announcing their AI pivots. Miners with orphaned capacity can still mine Bitcoin instead, to maximize powered land while they wait. Perhaps the election reinforced the value of that optionality.

Assessing Data Center Risk After a Texas Surprise
While the markets were pricing in a Democratic takeover of both the House and the Senate to some extent, we believe the magnitude of the win was unexpected. Most notably, a new Democratic Governor in Texas was not our base case, we think this introduces new questions and greater uncertainty for many PSPs operating in that region. We believe states with available power and comparatively lower near-term political risk, such as North Dakota, Louisiana and Kentucky, could stand to benefit from a potential moratorium on Texas data centers.

All Eyes on Texas: Texas holds ~30% of data center capacity currently under construction nationally, and Governor-elect Hinojosa has floated a broad moratorium on new sites until new legislation can be put in place. With the scope, mechanism and timeline all undefined, we expect greater uncertainty to continue to drive a risk-off reaction to many Texas based operators. Governor Abbott currently has two months left in office and retains the ability to push project approvals through before handoff, a dynamic that could favor operators who are already energized or sit at the front of ERCOT's interconnection queue.

Key Questions the market is Asking:
Scope and mechanism of a moratorium: Would it cover only new applications or also projects under      construction or with an interconnect agreement in hand?
PUCT Control: With two seats expiring in September 2027, could Hinojosa's appointments change the trajectory of ERCOT into 2028?
Fate of the ERCOT Process: Will ERCOT's interconnection process continue as planned?
Energization dates: Is a reasonable base case that the mega projects with energization dates in proceed as planned?
Grandfathering of executed agreements: For sites planned in 2H27 and beyond, is a signed PPA or interconnection agreement protected from retroactive review or do those publicly committed project timelines still hold if tenants are already secured (such as HUT's Beacon Point Phase 2 project with a signed tenant)?
Sales-tax repeal bill: With the bill already advancing in the Senate under GOP control, will the trajectory change under a Democratic governor?

The bull case for oil from the Saudi Aramco conference call yesterday:

“Since disruptions began, the global market has lost over 3 billion barrels of liquid supply. Alternative flows including export via our East-West pipeline and strategic petroleum reserve releases have narrowed the cumulative deficit to around 2 billion barrels. The remaining gap was balanced by demand management and substantial withdrawals from commercial inventories. While these actions have bought time, they are not a permanent solution.”

“The resulting market tightness is increasingly evident in physical prices. Buyers competing for immediately available barrels have driven physical prices above futures, and strong demand with constrained supplies has pushed refining margins to record levels.”

“Looking ahead, the market faces additional pressure from both seasonal and structural demand. Global product stocks are now alarmingly low, particularly for diesel, and with diesel demand expected to increase further in Q4, the market faces further pressure heading into winter. In 2027, global liquids demand is projected to expand by around 2.4 million barrels per day as demand management measures ease.”

“Beyond meeting additional demand, the market also faces the challenge of replenishing depleted inventories. More oil will be needed to rebuild inventories and fill additional storage capacity, a process which could take up to two years.”

tweets.text:
There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

Tim Dillon Explains the Democrat Sweep: “We have an economic war that's disguised as a culture war… Nobody wanted to go war with Iran... If people can't own a house, get married, have children, live, they're going to become radicalized in some way to some end of the political spectrum. That's obvious.”

Chamath:

“What is this? Is this a vote for Democrats? Is this a vote against Trump? Is it a vote against the cost of living? How do you interpret it?”

Tim Dillon:

“It's been said before, we have an economic war that's disguised as a culture war.

I think people that don't have the confidence in their economic standing are attaching meaning to a lot of things culturally, where there is none.

And I think it's a vote against the cost of living.

I think it's a vote against, in some ways, the corruption that people see is inherent in the system right now, that Donald Trump won claiming that he was going to correct.

I think it's a vote against what Donald Trump unfortunately has become, which is the system.

The same people that elected Trump because they wanted cheaper gas, cheaper groceries, they didn't want to go to war with Iran. Nobody wanted that. 10 people wanted it, and they gave Trump a lot of money.

I think it's a vote, a little bit, against people's circumstances, their economic circumstances.

And that's why people vote, and that's why I think you're going to have a massive shift to the Democrats.

If people can't own a house, get married, have children, live, they're going to become radicalized in some way to some end of the political spectrum. That's obvious.

You're not talking only about the poor people, or the working poor, or even the working class. There's a lot of white collar college graduates that are voting for the DSA candidates because they're mired in debt, they don't own anything, and they don't feel like they ever will.

And Trump was supposed to address those concerns, and if he doesn't, somebody else will.”

I don't know what the future will bring. A world where the situation with Iran does not improve, already historically low crude inventories evaporate, refined products blow up and the ensuing unrelenting inflation pushes the Fed and other central banks from hawkish to very hawkish, ending this cycle, is definitely feasible. 

However, there's a ton of AI doom in the air, last week's deleveraging and the recent crash across momentum assets are historical outliers, post-midterm price action was very positive (it reminded me of a miniature version of Trump's 2016 victory), high-risk earnings are mostly behind us, the front end of the Treasury curve already has two more hikes priced in by March, Brent is at 102, and the blue sweep should reduce war-risk premia (lower odds of Trump going wild in the Middle East - if he did, the Senate could revolt against him, and the odds of a House impeachment turning into a Trump removal would no longer be zero, though still small).

Therefore, I think it is time to go risk-on and bet on historical post-midterm seasonality with a 3 month horizon. I like Mag 7 (ex TSLA, too soon to fade the midterms), solar energy, and I continue to like long bonds as a growth-scare hedge. Among data centers, I like those with no Texas exposure (TeraWulf), as Texas unexpectedly electing a Democrat Governor reshapes the landscape. 

Good luck trading

I don't think engineers will start from a blank file anymore. They will point a swarm of agents at a problem like building a website and watch them work.

Agents  open the best apps in a real browser. They inspect the DOM, dump every network request, and map the backend. They use computer use to click through every flow like a real user. Then they rebuild it, piece by piece, while you watch the code appear.

And then agents plug in customer telemetry. The agents read customer feedback in the inbox. They ship dozens of features, they run A/B tests live, see what sticks, and kill the rest. Unit tests, performance, and load times get checked on every change.

The loop never stops. I made this video to show what I have in mind. The hard part won't be writing the code anymore. It will be knowing what's worth building.

tweets.text: Anyone thinking that last night's Democratic midterm sweep means an AI Freeze law or a Superintelligence ban like Bernie's are now possible is not being realistic, in my opinion. Even if such a bill did pass, President Trump would veto it, and Democrats do not have the supermajority needed to override him. Even in the unlikely scenario that enough Republicans defected to override a veto, President Trump would then decline to enforce an AI Freeze law by arguing that it unconstitutionally infringes on his Article II authority as Commander-in-Chief to protect national security.
